sections.report:
I reviewed the whole-piece section of the checklist against the screenshot. The image is about one screen, so I worked from it directly and didn't run the crop script. One line came out as a minor no.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something? — No.**
   - **Where:** "Export as file" is the first of the four buttons, at about x 276–437, y 298–356.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The heading asks a yes-or-no question: save the changes to the shared calendar or not. "Export as file" isn't an answer to that question. It's a separate task. Because it sits first in the row and looks exactly like the real answers, the viewer has to read and rule it out before they can decide. A two-way decision becomes a four-way scan, and the leftmost spot (where many readers start) goes to the least relevant choice.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 8 (aesthetic and minimalist design): every element on the screen supports the user's main task, and secondary content that competes with it is removed or demoted.
   - **Fix:** Take export out of this dialog, for example into the editor's menu. If it has to stay, demote it to a plain text link set apart from the decision buttons. Then the row holds only the answers to the heading's question.
   - **Kind:** Convention.
   - **Weight:** Minor on its own. The bigger cost comes from all four buttons looking the same, which belongs to the hierarchy and interface sections. Removing export makes that problem smaller but doesn't fix it.

**What's working.**
- **The heading asks the exact question the buttons answer.** "Save changes to the shared calendar?" says what the action is and what it affects. The text below it says why it matters: everyone who follows the calendar will see the new choir rehearsal times. A first-time viewer can say in one sentence what this dialog is for. (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*: self-evident.)
- **The style holds together.** One sans-serif typeface, one blue, the same rounded corners on the card and the buttons, and a soft shadow. Nothing looks borrowed from another system, and the calm, plain tone suits a routine save.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (every element does a job).

**First read:** The eye lands on the bold headline "Save changes to the shared calendar?" at y≈192. It moves to the one-line explanation, then reaches four identical blue buttons and has nowhere to settle among them. It reads as a confirmation dialog in a calendar app.

**Job (assumed):** Confirm or discard edits to a shared calendar that other people follow.

**Walk: What matters first**
- One element stands clearly above the rest: yes. The headline, at about 28 px bold and near-black, is the largest and darkest text.
- Each text level is distinct, with no near-duplicate sizes: yes. There are three levels: headline about 28 px bold, body about 17 px regular, button labels about 16 px bold in white on blue. Body and labels are close in size, but they differ in weight, colour and container, so they don't collide.
- Headings differ from body text in more than size: yes. The headline is bold, the body is regular.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline (x≈280–836, y≈175–210) is a full step above the body in both size and weight, and the body is the only other plain text. The eye starts in the right place and gets the question before the consequence.
- The text uses few sizes: headline, one body line and button labels. Each level does one job, so the hierarchy holds without effort.

*Note for the director:* The four buttons at y≈298–355 (Export as file, Discard changes, Keep editing, Save changes) look identical in fill, size and weight. Nothing marks "Save changes" as the main action, and nothing sets "Discard changes" apart as the destructive one. That is a hierarchy problem inside the controls, so under the checklist's rules it belongs in the Interface section, not here. It is the main problem on this screen.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've finished the checks and opened the reference entries; here is the arrangement report.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. It's a single confirmation dialog of 1280 × 800 px.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups?** No, not in the button row (y 298–355).
   - **Where:** the four buttons are spaced evenly, about 16 px apart: "Export as file" (x 276–437), "Discard changes" (453–644), "Keep editing" (660–816) and "Save changes" (832–1000).
   - **What the viewer meets:** "Export as file" is a side action and doesn't answer the question "Save changes?". The other three do answer it. With equal gaps, the row reads as four equal choices, so the viewer has to read every label to sort the answers from the extra option. "Export as file" also takes the leftmost, first-read position.
   - **Why:** equal gaps everywhere erase the groups (Wertheimer's proximity principle, via Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II "Shape").
   - **Fix:** split the row with space. Move "Export as file" to the far left with a clear gap, or out of the row altogether. Keep "Discard changes", "Keep editing" and "Save changes" together as one tight group on the right.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, minor. The bigger cause of the four-equal-choices reading is that all four buttons look the same, and that belongs to the Interface and Hierarchy sections, not this one.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge it shares with another, or clearly off it?** No.
   - **Where:** the left edge of "Export as file" sits at about x 276, while the heading and body text start at about x 280. The button row also reaches x 1000, past the body text's right end at about 988.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the button row sticks out about 4 px to the left of the text column. That's too little to look deliberate and just enough to look slightly off.
   - **Why:** a placement that is neither clearly on nor clearly off makes the eye waver (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). The idea that a break must read as deliberate has no confirmed source, so treat that part as common sense.
   - **Fix:** line up the button edges, or the button text, with the x 280 text edge. Or set the row on the text column's edges.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, minor. The 4 px is measured by eye from a crop, so check it in the live CSS.

**What's working.**
- **Spacing in the text block:** the heading sits close to the line it introduces (about 20 px), and there is a clearly bigger gap (about 40 px) before the buttons. Question, explanation and actions read as three steps in order.
- **Placement and padding:** the dialog is centred and sits in the upper part of the screen, which is the convention for a modal. Its padding is about the same on all sides (about 49 px left and right, 50–57 px top and bottom), so the card feels settled.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The 400 px of empty white below the dialog could be the blank page behind it, or a missing dimmed backdrop. Check in a live browser whether the modal has a backdrop that separates it from the page.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; exact alignment with no near-misses)

Walk (working notes): the image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I didn't run the crop or entries scripts. The text is a bold heading of about 28 px, one body line of about 17 px in dark grey, and four bold white button labels of about 16 px on blue. Every line comes out yes:
- Body text large enough: yes. It's about 17 px, larger than the button labels.
- Captions and labels: yes, there are none smaller than the buttons.
- Plain upright paragraph face: yes.
- One typeface plan: yes, a single sans in two weights.
- Small text weight: yes.
- Contrast: yes. Near-black on white, and white on mid-dark blue looks well over 4.5:1.
- Text over a photo or gradient: yes, there is none.
- Line length: yes. The single body line runs about 82 characters, but it's one sentence, not a paragraph.
- Leading: yes, a single line.
- Multi-line heading: yes, the heading is one line.
- Flush left: yes.
- Justified text: yes, there is none.
- Rag: yes.
- Widows: yes.
- Line breaks: yes.
- Paragraph marks: yes.
- Left edge: yes, the heading and body share one left edge at x≈280.
- Chunking: yes.
- Mixed case: yes.
- Emphasis: yes.
- Display spacing: yes. At 28 px the heading is at the edge of display size, and its default tracking reads cleanly.
- Kerning: yes.
- Tracking: yes.
- Capitals letterspaced: yes, there are none.
- Ligatures: yes. "file" in "Export as file" is 16 px button text, not large type.
- Real cuts: yes.
- Quotes and dashes: yes, there are none.
- Tabular figures: yes, there are none.
- Real type: yes.
- Nothing clipped: yes.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The type scale is tight and clear: three sizes with plain jobs. There's a bold heading of about 28 px, a regular body line of about 17 px, and bold button labels of about 16 px. Weight, not another size, separates the body line from the buttons, as Refactoring UI advises ("bolder, not bigger"). Each level reads as a different job at a glance.
- The heading (y≈192) and the body line (y≈244) share one left edge at x≈280. The body line is near-black on white, so it has full contrast. The question and its consequence read as one block in two quick fixations.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** No. The blue covers little of the page, but it is the only accent and it fills all four buttons the same way: "Export as file" (x≈276–437), "Discard changes" (≈453–644), "Keep editing" (≈660–816) and "Save changes" (≈832–1000), all at y≈298–356. When the accent is everywhere, it marks nothing. Someone answering "Save changes to the shared calendar?" sees four controls of equal weight. Color gives no hint which one answers the question. It also doesn't separate the safe choices from the one that throws work away ("Discard changes"), so they have to read all four labels before they act, and a wrong click is easy. This breaks the accent-restraint convention (Apple, *Human Interface Guidelines: Color*; Material Design 3, color roles): one accent for the main action. The fix: keep the solid blue for "Save changes" only. Draw "Keep editing" and "Export as file" in a neutral style, such as a gray outline or text button. Give "Discard changes" a neutral style too, or a red text treatment if your system has a destructive role. Then the action that answers the question is the one the eye lands on. Convention, and a defect in effect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The palette is small and controlled: white, one cool gray for the card border and shadow, near-black text, and one deep blue. Nothing is a stray one-off hue, so once the button colors are fixed the dialog will look like part of a system.
- The blue is dark enough that the white bold labels stand out clearly, with no shimmer at the edges. The card's value structure (dark title, mid-dark body, white card on a white page, separated by border and shadow) still holds up in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (strong color kept to a small share: the one accent fills all four buttons)

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image is a confirmation dialog for saving changes to a shared calendar. It has no chart, no table of figures and no dashboard.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

**Section.** Interface: applies. The image is a confirmation dialog with four buttons.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower? No.** All four buttons at y≈298–356 ("Export as file" x≈276–437, "Discard changes" 453–644, "Keep editing" 660–816, "Save changes" 832–1000) have the same solid blue fill, white bold label, size and corner radius. The heading asks a yes/no question, but nothing shows which button is the answer. The eye moves along the row and the user has to read all four labels before acting. That is a real cost in a dialog that publishes changes to other people. The usual rule is one filled primary button, with the other actions as outlined or text buttons (Material Design dialogs; Apple HIG; Refactoring UI). Fix: keep "Save changes" as the only filled button and move it to the right end, where it already sits. Make "Keep editing" a secondary outlined or text button, and push "Export as file" down further still. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Is each destructive action (delete, remove, reset) set apart from the safe actions, so it cannot be hit by mistake? No.** "Discard changes" (x≈453–644) throws away the user's edits. It looks exactly like the other buttons and sits about 16 px from "Keep editing" (x≈660), which is the safe way out. A user who means to back out can land on Discard, and nothing marks it as the one that loses work. The copy also never says whether discarding can be undone. Fix: style Discard as a destructive action (red text or outline, not a filled button), separate it from Keep editing (for example, group it on the left away from Cancel/Save), and if it is permanent, say so or offer undo (Nielsen 3 and 5). Defect. Weight: major.
3. **Are rare or advanced options kept behind a visible control, with the main content first? No.** "Export as file" (x≈276–437) has nothing to do with the question "Save changes to the shared calendar?". Yet it comes first in the row, in the left-most spot where the eye starts, with full primary styling. It makes four choices where the decision needs two or three, and it pulls attention away from that decision. Fix: take it out of this dialog and offer export from the calendar's own menu. If it has to stay, make it a low-weight text link set apart from the decision buttons. Convention (progressive disclosure, Nielsen Norman Group; Material dialogs keep actions to the decision at hand). Weight: minor on its own, but it makes finding 1 worse.

**What's working.**
- The labels are verbs that say what happens. "Save changes" repeats the heading's words, and "Keep editing" is a clear way out, so the user never has to work out an "OK" or "Cancel". This follows Nielsen 2 (match the real world) and Apple HIG on button titles.
- The body line says what saving does and to whom: everyone who follows this calendar. That is the consequence the user needs before publishing.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicator. A still can't show where focus lands when the dialog opens or how visible the focus ring is. Check that focus opens on a safe button, not "Discard changes", and that the ring is at least 2 px with 3:1 contrast.
- Whether Esc or a click outside the dialog closes it as "Keep editing".

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (one primary action; destructive action set apart; rare options behind a control), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).

Note: I couldn't open the catalog entries for these lines because my Bash calls were denied, so the sources above are cited from the approved source list rather than the entries' approved fix wording. The image is 1280×800, so I didn't need crops.
